title: Framing and cropping — Image Wiki
text:
Framing and cropping
  The frame is a decision about what is in the picture and what is not. The crop is the cheapest powerful edit there is — which also makes it the easiest way to throw the subject away.

  
    Termframing / cropping
    Also calledthe frame, crop, framing device, frame within a frame, aspect ratio
    Not the same ascomposition in general, focal length, zoom, negative space
    Read9 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Aspect ratio is a constraint, not a presetFraming inside the frameWhere the edge fallsBoth instructions are correctCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Two people stand shoulder to shoulder on the same pavement, point their phones at the same street, and come away with different pictures. Nothing in front of them differed. The only thing either of them decided was a rectangle.
The frame is that decision, and it does three jobs. It includes. It excludes — which is the same act, and the one people forget they performed. And it invents relationships that do not exist outside it: two things that land near each other in the rectangle are read as belonging together, whether they are two metres apart or two hundred. Your grouping machinery has the flat picture and nothing else (Gestalt grouping).
That third job is the one worth watching. A stranger thirty metres behind your subject becomes the person your subject is looking at. A chimney on the next street becomes part of this roof. A bright shop sign at the border becomes a comment on the face beside it. None of those relationships were in the world; the rectangle made them, and it makes them every time.
Cropping is framing done afterwards, with less freedom and no travel. Cambridge in Colour is blunt about how much it can still buy: you can resurrect an old photograph with nothing more than a crop (SRC-022).


The frame as Vachon made it: two girls, a mailbox, a rolled newspaper
Our own tight crop of the same negative


John Vachon, Ozark children getting mail from RFD box, Missouri, May 1940. Farm Security Administration, Library of Congress; public domain. The right panel is our own crop of the left one; nothing else was changed.
Left is about the mail. The open box, the rolled newspaper in her raised hand, the row of neighbours' boxes cut off by the top edge, the second child watching from behind her shoulder — every one of those is a decision to keep something.
Right is a good portrait of a girl, and it is not a better or a worse picture. It is a different one. The box, the newspaper and the errand are gone; so is the second child, and so is the reason the first one is smiling at somebody. Cropping tighter always improves something — here it removes two real competitors for attention — and the bill is paid in subject matter.


Aspect ratio is a constraint, not a preset
The frame's shape decides which compositions are available to you at all, before you point the camera at anything.

1:1squareroom above the tree, ground below the feet3:2the 35 mm framethe tree only just fits2.35:1cinema scopethe tree cannot fit, and the foreground is gone

Same scene, same scale, same width, all three centred on the same point. The only variable is the frame's proportion.
The square has room above the tree and ground below the feet, so it can be about a place. The 3:2 frame — 35 mm film, and most cameras since — only just holds the tree. In 2.35:1 the tree cannot fit at all and the foreground has gone: you can have the height or you can have the width, and the ratio has already chosen.
There is nothing aesthetic in this. It is arithmetic, and it is why the same subject wants a different position in each of the three.


The real numbers are worth carrying: 3:2 from 35 mm film, 4:3 on most phones and compacts, 4:5 for the classic portrait print, 1:1 for square, 16:9 for video, about 2.39:1 for widescreen cinema. A vertical subject in a 16:9 frame has two options, both bad — cut it, or make it small — and neither is a failure of composition. It is a mismatch between the subject and the rectangle, decided before the shutter.
Framing inside the frame
You can also build a second frame out of the scene: an arch, a doorway, a window, a gap in foliage. Photographers call it a frame within a frame and it is one of the standard moves (SRC-024).



Pieter de Hooch, The Courtyard of a House in Delft, 1658 (National Gallery, London). Public domain.
Count the frames. The painting's own edge; then the brick arch on the left with its dated tablet above it; then, deep in the passage, a second arch; then the bright window at the end of it. Four rectangles nested inside one another, and that nesting alone builds the depth — no perspective trickery required, just one shape overlapping the next, which is the most basic depth device there is (POST-001-SUP1).
Look at what the arch buys for the woman standing in the passage. She is small, she is turned away, her dark bodice barely separates from the wall — and you find her instantly, because she is the only thing inside an enclosure and she has the frame's brightest patch directly behind her.
Then look at the cost, because it is real. The arch is a wall as well as a window: your eye goes into it, arrives at the far window, and has to be dragged back out to the woman and child on the right. The picture is two compartments rather than one room.


An interior frame also stops the eye leaking out of a corner, which is why photographers reach for a branch across the top. Photography Life is honest about the failure mode: a tree that has no reason to be there, added because a frame was wanted, just looks insincere (SRC-020).
Where the edge falls
The edges are where a frame is won or lost, and a small distraction near the border costs far more than the same distraction near the middle (SRC-021). Part of the reason is mechanical: the border is the hardest, straightest, highest-contrast line in any picture, so anything that lands on it inherits that line's attention. Three failures with names:
Cutting a figure at a joint. Wrist, elbow, knee, ankle, waist.

kneeCut at the jointthe bottom edge lands on the kneesthe legs read as ending, not as continuingkneeCut between jointsthe bottom edge lands mid-thighthe legs read as running on out of frame

One figure, one scale, one position. The only variable is where the bottom edge lands.
Cut at the knees and the legs read as finished — the body looks complete and short of a part. Cut mid-thigh and the same legs read as continuing out of the frame. Your visual system completes what the border interrupts, and it takes joints as natural places for a body to end; a cut between joints gives it nothing to end on, so it keeps going.


Amputating something at the border. A hand, a foot, the tip of a spire, one wheel. The rule of thumb that works: either keep it clearly inside or cut it decisively. The half-measure — a boot with its toe just gone, a peak that almost touches the top edge — is the version that nags (SRC-017).
Cropping so tight the subject has nowhere to look. A face pressed against the border it is facing reads as blocked. Leave the space on the side the subject faces or moves toward, and it reads as about to (Negative space).



Gustave Caillebotte, Paris Street; Rainy Day, 1877 (Art Institute of Chicago). Public domain.
The decisive cut, made on purpose by a painter who could have put the border anywhere he liked. At the right edge a man in a top hat is sliced from crown to boots — roughly half of him, umbrella included, is outside the picture. Nobody reads that as a mistake. It reads as a street that carries on past the canvas, and the pedestrian traffic in the frame becomes a sample of something larger.
Compare it with the near-miss he avoided. Had that man been shifted a hand's width to the left, with only a shoulder and a sliver of hat clipped off, the eye would go straight to the damage. Cut a lot or cut nothing.
Note the lamp post while you are here: a hard vertical almost exactly on the centre line, dividing the canvas into a near half and a far half. A frame does not only have four edges; anything running from top to bottom acts as one.


Both instructions are correct
Fill the frame is right when the subject's own surface is the subject: a face, a texture, a hand, a market stall. Getting closer removes context, and removing context is the point.
Leave room to breathe is right when the subject's relationship to its surroundings is the subject: scale, isolation, direction, a place. Photography Life's version of the same advice is to keep important things off the far edges and to give subjects space they can occupy without crossing each other (SRC-021).
They only look like a contradiction because the word "better" is missing an object. Ask better at what, and one of them answers.
Common mistakes

"Cropping is what you do when the composition failed." It is a compositional tool of its own, and often the strongest one still available. It is also the only one you get on somebody else's photograph.
"A tighter crop is a stronger picture." Tighter raises tension and destroys context. Both of those are consequences, not improvements.
"Zooming in is the same as cropping." For what is in the frame, yes. For perspective, no — the relative sizes of near and far things are set by where you stand, not by the crop.
"The subject is what matters; the edges are trim." The edges decide whether the eye stays. That is why a vignette works at all (SRC-021).
"A frame within a frame always adds depth." It adds an enclosure. If nothing worth finding is inside it you have built a doorway to an empty room.


Checking a frame

Name one thing that was excluded. If you cannot, nobody chose the boundary.
Walk all four edges with your eye. Anything cut at a joint, half-amputated, or just touching?
Does the frame's shape suit the subject, or is a tall thing lying down in a wide rectangle?
If the subject faces or moves somewhere, is there room in that direction?
Try covering the outer tenth of the picture with your hands. If it improves, the crop is not finished. If the subject suddenly feels cornered, it already went too far.
